passage: Darshan wanted to run before college in the mornings, but in the first week he managed it only once. His shoes were in the tin trunk under the stairs, the socks somewhere else, and by the time he'd found both, the bus to Sinnar was due. So on Sunday he changed the setup. He put the shoes, socks tucked inside, right beside his charpai, and told himself the goal was only ten minutes: to the Hanuman temple at the end of the lane and back. "Ten minutes?" his friend Madhav scoffed. "That's not running." But on Monday Darshan's feet touched the shoes the moment he woke. He ran to the temple and back. Four weeks later he was still going, sometimes further, but never less than the temple.

qa.q: Where did Darshan put his shoes on Sunday?
qa.a: Right beside his charpai, with the socks tucked inside.

qa.q: Why was Darshan happy to set such a small goal despite Madhav's scoffing?
qa.a: Darshan wanted a start easy enough to happen every day; after a week of failed tries, ten minutes felt achievable rather than embarrassing.

qa.q: Which two choices helped the habit survive its first weeks?
qa.a: Keeping the shoes where his feet land on waking, and making the target tiny, to the temple and back, so there was nothing to hunt for and little to dread.

qa.q: How might Madhav's view change after four weeks?
qa.a: Madhav, who laughed at ten minutes, may be surprised that Darshan is still running and sometimes going further.

grounding: A student lowers friction by keeping shoes by the bed and setting a ten-minute target, and the running habit lasts.

passage: Anders had tried to start running three times since moving to Uppsala for university, and each time it died in the second week. Dark mornings, a cold floor, shoes lost somewhere in the hall cupboard. This time his flatmate Emil suggested something different. "Make it stupidly easy." So every night Anders laid out his running tights, jacket and shoes on the chair by his bed, and set the target at ten minutes on the lake path, nothing more. On the first morning he nearly skipped it, but everything was right there, so he pulled on the tights still half asleep. Ten minutes felt almost too short. He came back pink-cheeked and a little proud. Three weeks later the chair still held his kit every night, and Emil had started joining him.

qa.q: Where did Anders lay out his running kit each night?
qa.a: On the chair by his bed.

qa.q: How did Anders feel after the first ten-minute run, and why?
qa.a: He felt a little proud; after three failed starts, doing it at all, even briefly, showed him this attempt might be different.

qa.q: Which choice made the first morning work when Anders nearly skipped?
qa.a: Having everything laid out the night before, so he could pull on the tights half asleep without any search or decision.

qa.q: What would change for Anders if Emil stopped joining him later?
qa.a: The kit on the chair and the small target would still carry the habit, since the ease of starting, not company, is what got it going.

grounding: A student lays out running kit by the bed and sets a ten-minute goal, which helps the habit survive its early weeks.

passage: In the girls' hostel at Nandini's college, the sports track opened at six, but Nandini's alarm usually lost to her blanket. Her roommate Sunaina, who ran every day, suggested a trick. "Keep your shoes by your pillow. Literally. And promise yourself only ten minutes." So Nandini put her shoes at the head of the bed and her track pants on the chair. The first morning she grumbled but stepped straight into them. On the track she jogged slowly for ten minutes and walked back. "That's it?" Sunaina teased. "That's it," Nandini said. The next week she began adding a lap, but only when she felt like it. The deal stayed ten minutes. After a month, the track guard knew her name.

qa.q: What time did the sports track open?
qa.a: At six.

qa.q: Why might Nandini have been happy to answer "That's it" to the teasing?
qa.a: She knew the small target was the point; keeping the promise to herself mattered more than impressing Sunaina, and it felt good to have gone at all.

qa.q: What choice kept the habit going once Nandini began adding laps?
qa.a: Keeping the deal at ten minutes and adding laps only when she felt like it, so a tired day never made starting feel too big.

qa.q: How might Sunaina see Nandini's progress over the month?
qa.a: Sunaina, a daily runner, may be pleased that the simple trick worked and enjoy seeing a roommate who used to lose to the blanket become a regular.

grounding: A student keeps shoes by the pillow and a ten-minute target, lowering friction so the running habit survives.

passage:
Dear Jyoti,
Remember how I said I'd start running in January and you bet me a samosa I'd quit by the 10th? The old me would have lost. Every morning I had to hunt for shoes, socks and a clean T-shirt, and by then my blanket had won the argument.
So here's what changed. Every night the shoes go right beside my bed, socks stuffed inside, T-shirt folded on top. And my goal is only ten minutes, once round the hostel block. Ten! Some days I feel silly, it's so small. But on the cold mornings those ten minutes are the only reason I get out at all, and most days I end up doing twenty.
It's week five. I owe you nothing. 😊
Love,
Ankita

qa.q: Where does Ankita put the running shoes each night?
qa.a: Right beside the bed, socks stuffed inside, T-shirt folded on top.

qa.q: Why does Ankita sometimes feel silly about the ten-minute goal?
qa.a: It seems almost too small to count, yet Ankita also knows that on cold mornings that small target is what makes getting out possible.

qa.q: Which change mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Laying everything by the bed and keeping the target to ten minutes; there is nothing to hunt for and nothing big to dread, so the start beats the blanket.

qa.q: What might Jyoti think on reading 'I owe you nothing'?
qa.a: Jyoti will probably laugh at losing the bet and be glad, maybe impressed, that the running has lasted into week five.

grounding: A student lays out running shoes by the bed and sets a ten-minute target, and the new habit survives its first weeks.

passage: Harish, you asked how I kept running this time when I quit three times last year? Okay. I'm Parul, and I am not a morning person. Last year I'd plan a proper five-kilometre run, and by day four I'd wake up, think five kilometres, and roll over. This time I did two things. First, I sleep in my track pants, and my shoes wait beside the bed with the laces already loose, so I can step straight in. Second, the promise is just ten minutes: out to the bus stand and back. Most days that's all I do. Some days I keep going. It's been two months now, and the shoes have left a faint mark on the floor tile. That mark makes me weirdly proud.

qa.q: What is Parul's ten-minute route?
qa.a: Out to the bus stand and back.

qa.q: Why did Parul roll over by day four last year?
qa.a: Picturing a full five kilometres made getting up feel huge, so staying in bed seemed like the reasonable choice in that sleepy moment.

qa.q: What two choices helped Parul's habit survive this time?
qa.a: Sleeping in track pants with loose-laced shoes by the bed, and promising only ten minutes; the start became nearly effortless and too small to argue with.

qa.q: What might Harish take from Parul's story?
qa.a: Harish might see that a new habit needs an easy start more than a big one, and try shrinking a goal of Harish's own.

grounding: A student sleeps in track pants beside ready shoes and promises only ten minutes, so the running habit lasts.
